title: Vasubandhu
hookLine: Asanga's brother, who wrote a great summary of the Abhidharma, then turned to "mind only"

cards: Asanga had a younger brother: brilliant, sharp in debate, and, at first, not impressed by his older brother's new Mahayana teachings at all. In fact, the old account says, he mocked them. His name was Vasubandhu.
Before he was done, he'd write a great handbook of Buddhist thought, and then become a voice for the very teaching he'd laughed at. A clever person who changed his mind in public.

teach.b: Vasubandhu studied the Abhidharma, the careful lists that break experience into its smallest parts: moments of mind, kinds of feeling, causes and conditions.

He gathered it into verses with his own commentary, the Abhidharmakosha, the Treasury of Abhidharma. Here and there in the commentary he quietly disagrees with the school he's summarizing. Even his handbook argues.
Then the turn. The Life of Vasubandhu, an old account kept in Chinese, tells it this way. Asanga, worried for his brother, sent word that he was ill.
That night he heard a Mahayana sutra being recited, and something in it reached him.

He saw he'd been wrong, and he was so ashamed of the words he'd spoken against it that he wanted to cut out his own tongue. Asanga told him no. The tongue that had spoken against the teaching could now speak for it.
So Vasubandhu turned to the Mahayana and wrote short, dense verses and commentaries on how the mind shapes what it sees: the teaching called mind only, which opens tomorrow.
Some later writers have wondered whether two different men named Vasubandhu lie behind all these books. Tradition remembers one. Either way, the story's lesson stays.
He didn't hide his old self.
He changed his mind, and put the same sharp tongue to new work.

how: Vasubandhu's Treasury of Abhidharma is studied in Tibetan monastic colleges and in East Asian Buddhist scholarship, and his later verse works are core texts of the Yogacara school.

games.q: you're Vasubandhu. you've just realized the teaching you mocked was right. what do you do?
o: say nothing and hope no one remembers.
cut out the tongue that mocked it.
use the same tongue to speak for it.
games.why: he wanted to cut out his tongue, but Asanga stopped him: use it differently. so he wrote for the teaching he had mocked.

practice: Bring to mind something you once said against a person, a place or an idea, and later saw differently.
No need to cut anything out: find one fair, true thing you could say in its favor now, say it silently once, and notice how it sits in the mouth.

wordCard.voice: Vasubandhu. Asanga's brother, who wrote the Treasury of Abhidharma, mocked the Mahayana, then turned to it and wrote on mind only. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit name of the teacher who wrote the Abhidharmakosha and turned to Yogacara.

carryVoice: Your line: he changed his mind. The same voice can be put to better work. Nine hundred sixty-two days now.
